content: 1. Guidelines for the prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care of HIV in key populations are available, addressing essential interventions for adults and adolescents living with HIV in resource-limited settings. 2. A global strategy for the prevention and control of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) from 2006 to 2015 emphasizes breaking the chain of transmission. 3. Specific guidelines focus on the prevention and treatment of HIV and other STIs among sex workers in lowand middle-income countries, as well as among men who have sex with men and transgender individuals, recommending a public health approach. 4. Regional guidelines for the management of sexually transmitted infections provide additional resources for healthcare professionals. 5. The 2015 guidelines for the treatment of sexually transmitted diseases, as well as resources from the British Association for Sexual Health and HIV, the International Union against Sexually Transmitted Infections, and the Australian Sexual Health Alliance, offer further insights into STI management. 6. Comprehensive cervical cancer control guidelines outline essential practices for prevention and treatment, including cryotherapy, large loop excision of the transformation zone, and cold knife conization for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) 2–3 and adenocarcinoma in situ. 7. WHO position papers on human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccines emphasize their role in cervical cancer prevention. 8. Vaccination is a critical component of HIV care, with individuals living with HIV assessed for vaccine eligibility at all stages of care. Vaccines are generally more effective and safer in those receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART) and with CD4 counts above 200 cells/mm³. 9. People with severe immunosuppression may face higher risks from live attenuated vaccines, while inactivated vaccines, though safe, may require additional doses or revaccination after immune reconstitution. 10. Transient increases in plasma HIV-RNA load have been observed following vaccination, but these are not clinically significant. 11. HIV-exposed infants, children, and adolescents should receive all routine vaccinations per national immunization schedules. Adults living with HIV are often recommended vaccines for influenza, hepatitis B, pneumococcal disease, and tetanus, with additional immunizations based on age, risk factors, or travel plans. 12. HIV infection increases the prevalence and severity of skin and oral diseases, particularly when CD4 counts fall below 200 cells/mm³, affecting up to 90% of individuals in resource-limited settings. 13. Adverse drug reactions involving the skin are significantly more common in people living with HIV, with prevalence increasing as immunodeficiency worsens. 14. Skin and oral manifestations of HIV can exacerbate stigma, as visible signs such as papular pruritic eruptions may lead to discrimination. 15. Kaposi sarcoma and other systemic diseases may initially present on the skin, requiring urgent ART to reduce mortality. Other conditions, such as candidiasis, can cause significant morbidity, including pain that limits the ability to take antiretroviral drugs. 16. WHO guidelines released in 2014 address the treatment of common HIV-associated skin and oral conditions in lowand middle-income countries, recommending HIV testing for individuals with unknown status presenting with these conditions. 17. People living with HIV are at increased risk of developing chronic noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) such as cardiovascular disease (CVD), hypertension, diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), kidney disease, and cancers. 18. The intersection of HIV and NCDs is influenced by increased survival due to effective ART, lifestyle factors, long-term ART complications, and aging-related conditions. 19. Chronic HIV care provides opportunities for assessing, monitoring, and managing NCDs, particularly through primary care, integrating interventions such as nutrition assessment, dietary counseling, smoking cessation, exercise promotion, and blood pressure monitoring. 20. WHO has defined a package of essential NCD interventions (WHO PEN) for primary healthcare in resource-limited settings, focusing on CVD risk assessment and management, including hypertension, type 2 diabetes, chronic respiratory diseases, and early detection of breast and cervical cancer. 21. Studies have shown that people living with HIV have a 40–70% higher risk of myocardial infarction and cerebrovascular disease compared to HIV-negative individuals of the same age and gender. 22. The mechanisms underlying the association between HIV and CVD include chronic immune activation, inflammation, immunodeficiency, and higher burdens of traditional CVD risk factors. 23. ART is beneficial in reducing HIV-related morbidity and mortality, despite potential CVD risks. Discontinuation of ART or detectable viral loads is associated with increased CVD events. 24. Routine CVD screening for people living with HIV is recommended in several clinical guidelines, with validated tools showing potential to improve health outcomes and cost-effectiveness. 25. However, current CVD risk tools often underestimate risk in people with HIV and require adjustment or validation for this population. 26. The D:A:D study group has developed a CVD risk algorithm incorporating HIV-specific factors, such as CD4 count and ART use, which improves prediction accuracy but has limitations due to differences in study populations. 27. WHO PEN interventions have shown cost-effectiveness in the general population of lowand middle-income countries, with pilot studies indicating significant reductions in CVD risk and promotion of healthy lifestyles. 28. Disparities in CVD care among people with HIV have been reported, with lower rates of aspirin use for prevention and fewer cardiovascular procedures or therapeutics following acute myocardial infarction compared to HIV-negative individuals. 29. Regular assessment and management of CVD risk among people with HIV are expected to result in more equitable and improved care outcomes.
